about: The instruments an ordinary person on Minjerribah actually meets, and what each one does to them or for them. This file is the hand-written half of the legislation lane: the list, the plain-English descriptions, the parts that bear on a person, and the judgement about whether an instrument mostly asks or mostly gives. The measured half, which is the size, the structure and the currency of each instrument, comes out of the published consolidation and is not written here.

not_advice.where_it_must_show: On every screen that names an instrument, beside the citation, not behind a menu and not in a footer a reader can scroll past.

method.what_is_measured: Pages, volumes, contents entries, distinct provision numbers, chapters, parts, divisions and schedules, all taken from the published consolidation itself.
method.what_is_written: The plain-English description, the parts that bear on an ordinary person, the bearing and the life events. These are judgements written against the same documents and they are marked as judgements.
method.what_is_not_here: The text of any Act. The consolidations run to tens of thousands of pages, they belong to their publishers, and the licence position differs between the two registers. This pack records the citation, the structure, the size, the description and a deep link.
method.counting_note: Contents entries and distinct provision numbers answer different questions. An Act that restarts its numbering, as the Constitution does between its covering clauses and its sections, has more entries than distinct numbers. Neither is presented as the other.
method.accuracy_note: The page counts are exact. The provision counts are close rather than exact: a contents entry whose title wraps onto a second line can be missed, and an Act that numbers items inside a schedule has those counted too. On the Constitution the method finds 132 of the 137 provisions it lists, which is the size of the error to expect. Nothing here should be quoted as the number of sections in an Act; it is a measure of how much there is to read.

instruments.what_it_does: The instrument that made the Commonwealth and set out what it may do. It creates the Parliament, the executive government and the High Court, lists the subjects the Commonwealth Parliament may make laws about, leaves everything else with the States, says that a State law inconsistent with a valid Commonwealth law has no effect to the extent of the inconsistency, and says that it can only be changed by a referendum in which a majority of voters and a majority of States agree. Almost nothing in it speaks to a person directly. Everything else in this list stands on it.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: It is why some of the fine print in your life says Commonwealth and some says Queensland, and why the two sometimes overlap on the same page.
It is why a referendum, and not an ordinary Act of Parliament, is needed to change certain things.
It is the reason a Commonwealth law wins when a State law and a Commonwealth law say different things about the same subject.
It carries the trade and commerce guarantee that goods and services move freely between the States, which is why a Queensland business can sell into New South Wales without a border tariff.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act that tells you how to read every other Commonwealth Act. It says that where a provision could be read more than one way, the reading that best achieves the purpose of the Act is the one to prefer. instruments.what_it_does: The Commonwealth's own criminal law, held in a Code that sits as a Schedule to a short Act. It sets the general principles of criminal responsibility that apply to every Commonwealth offence, which is to say what has to be proved about a person's conduct and their state of mind, and then creates the offences the Commonwealth rather than the State prosecutes: fraud against the Commonwealth, offences involving money, drugs at the border, telecommunications and online offences, terrorism, and offences against Commonwealth officials.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: Fraud on a Commonwealth agency, which includes lying on a payment claim.
Offences committed using a carriage service, which is the law behind most online threat, stalking and image-based abuse charges.
Importation offences, which is why the customs question at the airport is a criminal one.
The general principles, which are what a prosecutor has to prove about intention or recklessness before any of it sticks.

instruments.what_it_does: The competition law, and inside it, as Schedule 2, the Australian Consumer Law. The competition half governs how businesses may deal with each other: cartels, misuse of market power, mergers, and access to essential infrastructure. The consumer half is the part that reaches a person every day. It prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct and unconscionable conduct, gives every purchase a set of consumer guarantees that cannot be contracted out of, sets remedies when a product fails, voids unfair terms in standard form consumer and small business contracts, and sets product safety and information standards.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The consumer guarantees, which mean goods must be of acceptable quality, match their description and be fit for the purpose you told the seller about. They are not a warranty, they cannot be signed away, and they last as long as is reasonable rather than as long as the receipt says.
The major failure rule, which decides whether you get to choose a refund or the seller gets to choose a repair.
Misleading or deceptive conduct, which is the workhorse of consumer complaints and applies whether or not anyone meant to mislead.
Unfair contract terms in the standard form agreements nobody reads: phone plans, gym memberships, insurance, storage.
Product safety recalls and mandatory standards.

instruments.what_it_does: The law behind every home loan, car loan, personal loan and credit card offered to a person for personal or household purposes. It requires anyone in the credit business to hold a licence and to act efficiently, honestly and fairly. It sets the responsible lending rules, which stop a lender writing a loan that is unsuitable for the borrower without first asking what they can afford. It carries the National Credit Code as a Schedule, which sets what has to be disclosed before you sign, what a statement must show, what a lender may charge, and what a borrower in hardship may ask for.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The hardship provisions, which let a borrower who cannot meet repayments ask the lender to change the contract, and require the lender to answer.
The pre-contractual disclosure that has to arrive before you sign, including the comparison rate.
The limits on what may be charged when a payment is late.
The requirement that the lender check the loan is not unsuitable, rather than leaving that entirely to the borrower.
The external dispute resolution scheme a licensee must belong to, which is free to the consumer.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act that governs what Commonwealth agencies and most larger businesses may do with information about a person. Its centre is a set of Australian Privacy Principles held in Schedule 1, which cover how information may be collected, what has to be told to a person when it is collected, what it may then be used for, when it may be given to somebody else, what has to be done to keep it secure, and a person's right to ask for it and to have it corrected. It also runs the credit reporting rules, requires notification when a data breach is likely to cause serious harm, and gives the Information Commissioner the power to investigate a complaint.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The right to ask any covered organisation what it holds about you, and to have it corrected if it is wrong.
The rule that information collected for one purpose is not to be used for a different one without consent.
Notifiable data breaches, which is why you get told when a company loses your details.
Credit reporting, which sets what may go on a credit file, how long it stays and what may be done about a default listed in error.
The small business exemption, which is the reason many businesses a person deals with are not covered at all.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act that gives a person a legally enforceable right to be given access to documents held by Commonwealth ministers and agencies, unless the document falls within an exemption. It sets how a request is made, what it may cost, how long an agency has to answer, and what may be withheld and why. It also requires agencies to publish a set of information about themselves without being asked, and gives a right to have a personal record corrected.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The right to ask a Commonwealth agency for its documents without giving a reason for wanting them.
Access to your own file, which is often cheaper and faster than the general right.
Internal review and then review by the Information Commissioner if access is refused.
The exemptions, which are where most of the argument happens: cabinet documents, personal privacy of other people, commercial value, and deliberative processes.

instruments.what_it_does: The national workplace law. It sets the National Employment Standards, which are the minimum conditions no agreement may go below: maximum weekly hours, requests for flexible working, parental leave, annual leave, personal and carer's leave, compassionate leave, community service leave, long service leave, public holidays, notice of termination and redundancy pay, and casual conversion. It provides for modern awards and enterprise agreements, sets the annual wage review that fixes the national minimum wage, creates general protections against adverse action taken for a prohibited reason, and gives an unfair dismissal remedy.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The National Employment Standards, which are the floor under every payslip in the country.
The modern award that covers your job, which sets your classification, your penalty rates and your allowances.
Unfair dismissal, which has a strict time limit measured in days rather than months.
General protections, which cover being treated badly for a reason such as making a complaint, taking leave or belonging to a union.
Casual employment, including the definition of a casual and the pathway to permanent work.

instruments.what_it_does: The goods and services tax. The tax invoice rules, which is why a receipt over a certain amount has to show particular things.
The quarterly activity statement, which is where a small business meets it.

instruments.what_it_does: Queensland's discrimination law, which covers more grounds in one Act than the Commonwealth covers in four. It prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on a list of attributes including sex, relationship status, pregnancy, parental status, breastfeeding, age, race, impairment, religious belief, political belief or activity, trade union activity, lawful sexual activity, gender identity, sexuality and association with someone with an attribute. instruments.what_it_does: The Act that lists a set of human rights and requires Queensland public entities to act compatibly with them and to give proper consideration to them when making a decision. It requires new legislation to be accompanied by a statement of compatibility, requires courts to interpret Queensland law compatibly with human rights so far as is possible consistently with its purpose, and allows a person to complain to the Queensland Human Rights Commission where a public entity has not complied. It does not create a free standing right to compensation.

The requirement to give proper consideration, which is a process right rather than a guaranteed outcome.
The right to be heard, which can be attached to an existing complaint about a decision.
The limitation clause, which allows rights to be limited where the limit is reasonable and demonstrably justifiable.

It gives the tribunal jurisdiction over minor civil disputes, tenancy disputes, body corporate matters, building disputes, guardianship and administration, anti-discrimination complaints referred to it, and review of a long list of administrative decisions. instruments.what_it_does: The Act that decides who pays for a fence and what may be done about a neighbour's tree. It sets the default that adjoining owners contribute equally to a sufficient dividing fence, sets the notice a neighbour must be given before fencing work, and provides a process to resolve disagreement. Cultural heritage management plans, which are required for some activities and available voluntarily for others.
Stop orders, which can halt work immediately.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act written for this island and no other. It set the framework for ending sand mining on Minjerribah, dealing with the existing mining leases and the transition off them, and providing for the progressive transfer of land to the protected area estate. It was amended in 2016 to bring the end date for mining back to the end of 2019.

It sits behind the land transfers that expanded the national park.
It is the instrument the State's transition funding programs were built around.
For a resident it is felt through employment, land tenure and rehabilitation rather than through any duty on them personally.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act that sets how Queensland prepares for and responds to disasters. It establishes local, district and State disaster management groups, requires disaster management plans at each level, provides for the declaration of a disaster situation, and gives declared disaster officers powers during a declaration including directing evacuation, controlling movement, and entering and taking control of property where necessary.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The local disaster management group, which is a council function and which plans for the community a person lives in.
Evacuation directions, which are lawful orders rather than advice once a disaster situation is declared.
Movement control, which is what closes a road or a crossing.
The obligation on a person to comply with a direction from a declared disaster officer.
The planning obligations, which exist before anything happens and are where the real work is.
instruments.key_provisions_note: None recorded. This record describes the Act by topic rather than by section number.
instruments.bearing_reason: It removes ordinary freedoms during an emergency and it is the reason there is a coordinated response at all. It is the clearest case in the list where a person willingly accepts a large restriction for a short period.
instruments.why_listed: An island with one vehicle ferry route, a bushfire history and a coastal hazard exposure is exactly the community this Act was written for.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act that governs public passenger transport in Queensland. It provides for the accreditation of operators and the authorisation of drivers, provides for service contracts under which the State buys scheduled services from operators, provides for fares and ticketing including concessions, regulates taxi and booked hire services, and sets the conduct rules and offences that apply on a public passenger service.

Driver authorisation, which is the check behind the person driving a bus, taxi or booked hire vehicle.
Conduct on a service, including the power to refuse or remove a passenger.
Accreditation of operators, which is the standard a small local operator has to reach.

instruments.what_it_does: The Act behind swearing an oath, making an affirmation, and signing a statutory declaration or an affidavit in Queensland. It sets who may take a declaration and witness an affidavit, what form the words take, and makes a false declaration an offence. It is the oldest instrument in this pack and it is met by nearly everybody at least once.
parts_that_bear_on_a_person: The statutory declaration, which is the form a person signs when an agency wants a fact confirmed and has no other proof of it.
Who may witness one, which is a defined list and is why a justice of the peace or a solicitor is needed.
The affidavit, which is the sworn document used in court proceedings.
The offence of making a false declaration, which is what gives the signature its weight.
instruments.key_provisions_note: None recorded. This record describes the Act by topic rather than by section number.
instruments.bearing_reason: It asks almost nothing of a person except honesty, and it gives them a way to prove something with a signature instead of a document they do not have.
instruments.why_listed: It is in the owner's own 2012 stack and it is the oldest Act here. It is also the one most people have used without ever knowing its name.
instruments.island_link: Finding an eligible witness on an island with no resident solicitor is a real access problem, and it is the same problem that makes an enduring power of attorney harder to execute here than on the mainland.
